findings.title: BuildIndex no longer single-flights a key, so concurrent builds race
findings.body: BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build, so GetIndex blocked until that key was published and a second caller reused the same index. The lock is now taken only to assign b.cache[key] after the build. getOrCreateIndex still does an unlocked check-then-build (GetIndex, then build if nil), and init can also call BuildIndex concurrently. Two callers for the same NamespacedResource therefore both miss the cache and both build. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory (one fails or they corrupt the path); for memory indexes both succeed and the later write silently replaces b.cache[key] without closing the first index. The discarded index never receives watch updates, while the caller that kept the other pointer searches a divergent copy. Cache publication also does not check whether an entry already exists, and TotalDocs ranges b.cache with no lock, so a concurrent insert is a concurrent map read/write that can panic.

findings.title: File index rebuild uses bleve.New and will fail every subsequent startup
findings.body: When size exceeds FileThreshold, BuildIndex always calls bleve.New on a stable directory under Root (namespace/resource.group). bleve.New creates a new index and returns an error if that path already exists; there is no bleve.Open fallback, and neither the error paths nor shutdown delete or close the directory. A successful on-disk build therefore leaves a directory that makes the next BuildIndex fail. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts server construction, so the second process start cannot bring unified storage up until that directory is removed by hand. A failed or crashed build poisons the same path the same way. The removed log even noted that the last resource version is not checked before recreating the index.

findings.title: Startup index workers share err and can swallow build failures
findings.body: init launches one goroutine per namespace via errgroup and each one does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` then `return err`, where err is the single variable from GetResourceStats, not a per-goroutine local. Those goroutines write and read err concurrently (data race). One worker can overwrite another's error with nil between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait can return nil even though a build failed. Init is now mandatory in NewResourceServer and a swallowed error lets the process start with a partial search index and no retry (server.Init is sync.Once). totalBatchesIndexed++ in the same closure is also an unsynchronized counter, so the "namespaces indexed" span attribute is wrong under the same workers.

findings.title: Search watch loop panics or spins after the event channel closes
findings.body: After indexing, init always starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` on context.Background(), ignoring the server cancel context. SQL WatchWriteEvents' poller closes that channel when the backend is stopped (backend.Stop cancels b.done, poller defers close(stream)). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. Even with a nil check the loop never exits, so it would busy-spin. This goroutine is now started for every search-enabled server at construction, not only after the first RPC, and nothing in Stop waits for it or stops it.

findings.title: Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed
findings.body: TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for bringing up the storage-server target, which now builds the unified-storage index inside InitializeModuleServer / NewResourceServer. This change skips the test entirely when GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. CI no longer exercises eager init, DB stats, or index build against Postgres, so a Postgres-only startup failure caused by moving Init out of the RPC path will not be caught.
